utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, 30th of November, 2009. First of all, my apologies for this delay, which is not to blame on us, but it is once again due to the Gotovina Chamber. And good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Scott and his case manager, and good afternoon to all the people assisting us. Mr. Registrar, you have four IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness 4D-AB. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC01130. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC01131. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC01132. And, finally, the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC01133. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. I am going to read out a short oral ruling on a motion for leave to file a reply. On the 23rd of November, 2009, the Praljak Defence filed a motion to seek for leave to reply to the Stojic Defence's and the Prosecution's responses to its motion to admit documentary evidence of the 26th of October, 2009. The Praljak Defence also sought to have an extension of time to file its reply until the 18th of December, 2009. The Praljak Defence wishes to respond to specific arguments which it deems erroneously raised by the Prosecution in its response. The Praljak Defence argues also that filing a reply will make it possible to correct errors that are found in its motion of the 26th of October, 2009. In light of the submissions by the Praljak Defence, the Trial Chamber decides to grant leave to file a reply. However, the Trial Chamber is of the view that extension until the 14th of December, 2009, is sufficient for the Praljak Defence to prepare and file the reply. So you have until the 14th of December, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have the witness brought in, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Witness, please state your surname and first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Filip Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of March, 1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired at the moment. I work in de-mining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are retired from the army, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was a professional officer, and I'm now retired from the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was your last rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you had an opportunity to testify in a court of justice as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia? And if so, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in the Kordic trial and the Cerkez trial before this Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you testified for whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kordic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, some information. You have already testified in the Kordic case, and I know you have because I have the entire transcript of your testimony in that case. It was public testimony. So you know how things are going to take place. First, you will answer questions by Ms. Alaburic. You must have met with her. She's going to put questions to you, and she will also submit documents that you can find in two binders. There's binder number 1 and binder number 2 that you have in front of you. When she wants to call a document, she'll give you the number, and you can find the document in question. When she's done with her questions - she is going to take four hours to do so, to ask the questions of you - then the other accused's counsel are going to ask questions as part of their cross-examination, following which the Prosecutor, who's on your right, Mr. Scott, will cross-examine you. I believe you have had an opportunity to be cross-examined in the Kordic case, where Mr. Nice, the famous Mr. Nice, was the Prosecutor in chief. You have four Judges in front of you. They can ask questions of you at any time to go into a document with further detail or because an answer you may give calls for some follow-up questions. They may also have questions that would be necessary for truth to come to light. You were a general, so normally you should be very rational and speak to the point, so do try to answer accurately any questions put to you. If you don't understand a question, do not hesitate for the question to be rephrased, even if it is a Judge asking you the question. And even if you notice that there is a mistake in the question put to you, do say so to the person asking it. Furthermore, we have breaks every hour and a half for 20 minutes. You are under oath. Therefore, you are now a witness of the Court. You're not supposed to have any contact whatsoever with anybody during the days of your testimony. Needless to say, you may contact your family, but you're not allowed to contact the press, the media, or lawyers. You are to testify on Monday and Tuesday of next week, according to the schedule, so I suppose you made all the necessary arrangements to stay here until the beginning of next week. Also, if at any time you're not feeling well - it can happen, it even happens to Judges - so do say so, raise your hand and ask for a break for you to have a rest. You never know, especially with the stress caused by the fact of testifying, you may feel unwell. It's never happened so far. So this is what I wanted to convey to you. Of course, we are available to you if you have any questions related to your testimony. This being said, you may proceed, Ms. Alaburic. I can see that you have the lectern, so you're ready to go, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to say good afternoon to you and everybody from the Prosecution, especially Mr. Scott. Good afternoon to the rest of the Defence counsel, to you, Witness, and to everybody else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Witness, we're going to start off with a short CV, but before I do that, let me ask you whether, about a year ago, a request came in from the Prosecution to conduct an interview with you before your arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was your answer to their request?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My answer was, yes, with the proviso that I did not wish to talk to -- well, if I can say some clerks, but to the Prosecutor, personally, if they wanted to contact me in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which name you mentioned from the Prosecution, which person you said you would accept talking to?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I might have known a name from the media, but I can't give you a name now. Ramak [phoen] or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, it was Mr. Scott, my colleague Mr. Scott. And since Mr. Scott is in the courtroom here today, I believe that he remembers that request of yours and that that is why he has decided to be in this courtroom here this afternoon. Now, General, let's describe your CV to the Trial Chamber and everybody else, your education, training, career, and so on. You told us that you were born in 1946?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Where were you born? In Travnik, Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was Yugoslavia at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to set out your CV, your education and career, so please listen to me and correct me if I'm wrong at any point. And if the information is correct, then confirm it, please. Now, as far as your education goes, this is what you have had: You graduated from the Military Academy in Belgrade, and you studied from 1966 to 1970. After that, you completed the Command Staff Academy in 1979 in Belgrade. Tell us, General, is that correct so far?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You started serving in the Yugoslav People's Army in Slovenia, and you spent four years there as a commander of a battery. Then you went to Doboj, which is a town in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you spent six years there as battery commander again. And then four years after that, you were the Chief of Staff of a regiment. Then you went to Derventa, another town in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you spent four years there as the Chief of Staff of the regiment there. So you held the same post there, too. And then you went back to Doboj and spent two years there as the regiment commander. And from 1990 until April 1992, you were in Sarajevo, the Chief of Staff of the artillery of the 4th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army. Tell us, please, General, is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the chief of artillery of the 4th Corps, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now your life's road was as follows: On the 8th of April, 1992, you left the Yugoslav People's Army. On the 10th of April, you arrived in the area of Travnik and Vitez. You spent a relatively short time there, performing the duties of commander of the Regional Staff of Bosnia. And after that you became the deputy commander of the HVO for the Central Bosnia Operations Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I thought Ms. Alaburic was going to ask that question, but she didn't, so I'll ask it. What was your rank in the JNA when you left it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was lieutenant-colonel. And that year, I was supposed to be promoted to colonel because I had all the necessary requirements, but I left as a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, anyway, in June 1992, you became commander of the tactical group or operative group for the Travnik-Novi Travnik-Vitez area in the Central Bosnia Operations Zone. In October 1992, you were appointed commander of the HVO Brigade in Travnik. And roughly until April 1993, you performed these three duties: Deputy commander of the operative zone, commander of the Tactical and Operations Group, and commander of the brigade. In April 1993, you were appointed to the joint command [realtime transcript read in error "commander"] of the BH Army and HVO, and you participated in the various commissions charged with looking into possibilities for quelling the conflict. In June 1993, you returned to the Vitez area and remained there, remained in that enclave, and fought there until roughly April 1994. In April 1994, you became commander of the Military District --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I was not going to interrupt counsel until she finished her question, but in the event that it might have been a transcription error or translation error, I just wanted to -- what we got on the transcript a few moments ago, it says: "In 1993, you were appointed to the joint commander of the BH Army and HVO and you participated in the various commissions ..." I believe perhaps what was intended was that he became -- he was appointed to a joint commission in Central Bosnia around that time. I'm not aware of -- unless counsel can provide us some additional information, I'm not aware of any joint command during that time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott is absolutely right, because in the Kordic case it was a question put to this witness. He was a member of a joint commission. But please ask your question again for this to be in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer ?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour will be able to tell you, but we prepared one of the documents in the set on joint command, and it is document 4D455, in which, to the joint command of the BH and the HVO, the following were appointed: Mario Andric, Filip Filipovic, and Zivko Totic. And so in this portion related to the joint command, our case will be that, yes, a joint command was established, in the sense that persons were appointed at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then at the levels of the corps or military districts, so that I was not wrong. I very consciously and intentionally said "joint command," but we can ask the witness to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So tell us, please, General, what were you in the spring of 1993? What posts did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Before the witness gives the answer, I do want the record to be clear, then. And I do appreciate counsel's candour. What counsel has just indicated was this is essentially an argumentative point. This is her interpretation, this is her characterisation of the relationship. Having worked in the Kordic case and having seen this testimony before, what was clearly described at the time was this was a joint commission which existed for a few weeks, met a few times. It had nothing to do with anything being like a joint command function. Now, I understand that counsel wants to argue her case, but this is an argumentative point that's being made now, and I believe all the prior testimony and evidence will indicate that what we're talking about here was a joint commission that existed for a very short time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I suppose that counsel is now going to ask an open question so that she will take account of your objection. I would, however, point out, too, a small but not insignificant difference. I think that counsel -- that in the record we read that he was appointed to the joint commander of the BH Army and HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said "joint command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading what I have in front of my eyes. Please, interpreters, do not take this as criticism, and I absolutely take your point. It's just that the record should be "command" on line 22 of page 8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, for that correction. I took on board Mr. Scott's objection, so where it read "joint commander," so it is "joint command." There were endeavours to set up a joint command, but there was a joint commission as well which toured the area of Jablanica and Konjic, and undertook a series of measures to bring the situation back to normal, which was very tense at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, let the witness answer, because you are now intervening as if it was him who was talking. Mr. Scott raised an objection, and he knows the Kordic case very well. You know that too. So please ask the witness whether he was part of a commission or whether he was a member of a joint command, or both at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I was in the commission. We toured positions, resolved problems. And then I was appointed to the joint command and personally went to Zenica to see the headquarters of the joint command. I met with Siber, Hadzihasanovic, Sefer, at Zenica, where it was support to be sited, and with them I went to Konjic. So the joint command was appointed. There was work done to set it up. To what extent it functioned, well, that's for us to elaborate upon later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assure you, Your Honours, that the general is following very closely what I'm explaining about his career, and he will correct me if I'm wrong. And my learned friend Scott, if they think that something is wrong, they can deal with that in their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, we stopped when you were appointed in April 1994 as commander of the Military District of Vitez and Mr. Kordic went to the Main Staff of the HVO. You stayed at that post for a year, and in April 1995 you are at the Military District of Tomislavgrad. But as soon as in May 1995, you go to the Joint Staff of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 31st of January, 2007, you retire from active military service, holding the rank of major general of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1998, you were the director of the De-mining Centre for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And from 2002 onwards, you volunteer in a humanitarian NGO which focuses on de-mining, and the name is Provita. General, please tell us whether the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For starters, while you were deputy commander of the Operations Zone of Central Bosnia, who was the first commander that you deputised at the time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My first commander was Zarko Tole.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How long did he occupy that post?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: For some 10 days before he was captured by the Army of Republika Srpska. I was deputy to Tole, then Mr. Zulu, for a very brief time, and then Blaskic became commander. He was number 1 and I was number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a couple of words about the activities of Zarko Tole as commander of the Central Bosnia Operations Zone. What were his first moves when he took over that position?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Zarko Tole arrived around mid-May, and before he met me he held a number of meetings at municipalities, and at such meetings he advocated the idea of joint struggle of Croats and Muslims. I encountered him in the municipality of Travnik, and since we knew each other from Derventa, it didn't take us long to agree. He said, You are going to be my deputy. We have meetings tomorrow at Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno. We will continue with our activities. And we went together to Bugojno, spent a couple of days there, and then he was captured by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, when, as a JNA officer, you came to the area of Central Bosnia, what was the reception that you encountered there by the local population?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Central Bosnia, the Lasva Valley - this is where I hail from - I encountered armed individuals. They were gladdened by my arrival because they thought that some professionalism will be injected into defence efforts, it will be improved. I knew some people in Vitez. I knew nobody at Busovaca. But I attended a meeting of the then crisis headquarters that I was supposed to command, the area of Bosnia minus Posavina, which is a huge area. And the circumstances were that I did not know many people in my home area, but I managed. Somehow I started creating the preconditions to set up an army because I was aware of the dangers that were lurking behind the horizon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases of lack of trust because of your JNA background?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, many occasions I encountered that. I came to that area as a traitor and a Communist, and I left the JNA rather late, after it had performed many negative deeds, but after a month I started being accepted as a commander, due to my efforts that I invested in that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you retired as a Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army as an HVO officer or taking another route?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As an HVO officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether the time you spent in the HVO was calculated towards your years of service and retirement entitlement as an FBiH Army officer?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, like in everybody else's case, and the time I spent in combat was counted as twice as long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm going to put a question to you which I've never put before. I could have done it before, but I didn't really have the opportunity. You were in the HVO, and then you joined the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where you had an official role. We have seen a number of HVO personalities who became representatives of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; Mr. Prlic, for example, who was minister of foreign affairs. When you joined the Federation, how was the climate, the environment? Did they welcome you or was it difficult? Could you tell us how you became integrated within the Federation? Was it done naturally or were there a lot of reluctant people? Could you tell us exactly what you felt at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is a bit vague, but I'll try to explain. When I came to the Travnik and Vitez area, I was accepted by everybody, both the Muslims and the Croats, and later on both the Territorial Defence and the HVO as commander, when it comes to combat operations and professional aspects of combat, meaning de-mining of the line of defence, deployment and disposition of forces, et cetera. And even the Mujahedin, in May 1992, accepted me as commander, in terms as I encountered them on the defence positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question wasn't clear, obviously you're not answering my question, because this is not what I asked. I am asking what happened when you arrived in your position within the Federation, but after the conflict. This is what I want to know. How were you welcomed after the conflict, after the Dayton Agreement, the Washington Agreement, and so on, when the Army of the Federation was set up? Within this army, there were former members of the BH Army and former members of the HVO, and I would like to know what the feeling was. Was it like other brothers-in-arms who found each other when at one point in time they had been enemies or not? What happened in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you specified 1994, after the Washington Accords. I was at that time deputy commander of the military district, and after a while commander of the military district or the corps. From 1992 and 1994, I both co-operate and combat -- fight those [as interpreted]. You will have to specify your question in terms of time. With General Alagic, in the first year of the war, I worked perfectly well and co-operated. Then the next year, we fought. And after the Washington Agreement, we then co-operated again. You will have to specify the time-period. When I came to the Joint Command of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, that was in 1995. Since I was the commander and my opposite number from the Muslim side, we worked perfectly, and 1995 was very successful in terms of liberating territory and bringing the war to an end. So your question should be more specific. How did I feel? Well, as well as I could in the circumstances, given the relations obtaining [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction. In the transcript, you said that I was minister of foreign affairs of the Federation. I just want to say that I was not Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina minister of foreign affairs, but Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was minister from 1994 to 1996. So this may have been a mistranslation. I'd like to rectify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Ms. Alaburic, you may pursue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to show you several documents. Let us go through them briefly to see how, from mid-1992, the HVO was deemed as an integral part of the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then we will see how it was legislated upon by the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Accords. You may listen to me, and I'm going to refer to those documents briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologies to Ms. Alaburic and the witness but I do want to make a record early on, and I will continue to object in the course of the direct examination, to any characterisations, introductions, of the nature of the witness's testimony and what the testimony -- what the witness is going to say next. Just now, Ms. Alaburic said: "I'm going to show you several documents," this all in front of the witness, of course. "Let us go through them briefly to see how, from mid-1992, the HVO was deemed as an integral part of the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then we will show how it was legislated upon by the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Accords." I don't think we need prefaces and introductions as to the points counsel wishes to make. Normal practice in the courtroom is that questions are asked and answers are given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, yes, you should have said, I will show you a number of documents, show the documents, and then you can conclude by saying, Well, according to the comments made from these documents, do you really mean that the HVO was a part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina? But you're putting the horse before the cart, and Mr. Scott is absolutely right when it comes to procedure. But continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought I would facilitate to everybody in the courtroom to make a preface to the topic, but I'm going to skip from theme to theme and leave it for people to find their bearings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the first document I'd like to ask you about is document P339. This is the Friendship and Co-operation Agreement between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. General, listen to me -- please listen to me. When I want you to take a look at a document, I'm going to indicate that. This agreement was signed on the 21st of July, 1992, by President Franjo Tudjman and President Alija Izetbegovic, and in the sixth paragraph it says: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is an integral part of the United Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council will have its representatives in the joint command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina." My question, General: Did you see yourself as a member of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what did you think -- what was the country that you were defending at the time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I took part in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was defending myself, my family, the local community, and the wider community in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know why you're asking me this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to explain, but I'm afraid that Mr. Scott would object to that. Let me go to the next document, 4D410, 4D410. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we just looked at a document that we have seen on numerous occasions, and the Judges know this document inside-out. As Ms. Alaburic just asked you, on item 6 in this document it says that the armed component -- that the HVO is an integral part of the united Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what's written on paragraph 6. This was signed by the president of the Presidency on July 21st, 1992. Now, I have a question which is of a legal nature and might be outside your scope of competence, but we know that the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina made a decision declaring the HVO armed forces illegal. Now, there's one thing I don't understand. On this we have, on the one hand, a document which is an international agreement, which could be ratified by the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but if this text goes against the Constitution, the Constitution needed to be changed because there's a hierarchy in legal standards. But the Constitutional Court still decided that the HVO and its armed component was illegal. Now, you were on the field at the time. Were you aware of the decision made by the Constitutional Court, and were you aware of this agreement signed between Tudjman and Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of agreements and high politics, this is something I learned about later. But all those documents, agreements, did not mean a thing for me when I spent hours every day being fired at. You have to understand this. I do not know how to formulate this in legal terms. As I said, I defended Bosnia-Herzegovina because it was internationally recognised as a state at the time. See, the Territorial Defence and later on the armija of BiH, HVO, or the Army of Republika Srpska, were either legitimate or illegitimate because they were working to defend their own people. I do not get the gist of your question. Three sides are in conflict with each other. The Territorial Defence and the HVO fought together, hand in hand, and the decisions of the Presidency, agreements, et cetera, they may be relevant today, but they were not at the time. I never considered myself as a paramilitary, as an illegitimate -- member of an illegitimate operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, the next document is 4D410. That is the Decree with the Force of Law on Changes and Amendments of the Decree with the Force of Law on Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was adopted by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was signed by Alija Izetbegovic. And in Article 1 of that decree, it reads: "The Republic's armed forces shall comprise the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and all the other units that are subsumed under the Supreme Command." General, did anyone take the floor away from you or bar you from working at any meeting because you were a member of the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody ever even thought that because I was a commander in the Croatian Defence Council, that they would challenge the function that I occupied until then. There was talk. They would say, You were a paramilitary to the others. Now, if I'm a paramilitary -- well, when you came across members of the Territorial Defence, but it had nothing to do with meetings or any relevant facts related to that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is P1329, and it's a joint statement dated the 27th of January, 1993, which was signed in Geneva by Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban. In point 1, it says that all conflicts between the BH Army and the HVO should stop. And in point 2, it says that without delay, a joint command should be established. Now, tell us, General, at that time or perhaps later on, did you ever come across any statements made by Alija Izetbegovic to the effect that the HVO was not a legitimate army of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to everybody else who joined up with that army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard any statements of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is P1988. This is an agreement which, on the 20th of April, 1993, in Zenica, was signed by Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic. In point 1 of this agreement, it says that: "The BH Army and the HVO are both legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are treated equally." This agreement was signed in the presence of General Morillon and Mr. Thebault. Tell us, please, General, at that time did you have a meeting with Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that already on the 20th, and certainly on the 21st and 22nd, there was a meeting in UNPROFOR, the UNPROFOR base in Vitez, but Morillon wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at that meeting in Vitez was Sefer Halilovic there?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, Dzemal Merdan, and others on the side of the TO, and Petkovic, myself, Blaskic, and others on the side of the HVO. And the meeting was conducted by Colonel Stewart, or was it Colonel Williams?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the representatives of the BH Army, did they try and reach an agreement with you, who were the representatives of the HVO, or did they come to Vitez, as an illegitimate and unlawful army, to disarm you and arrest you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Problems were resolved on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, current problems, and in the Lasva River Valley, Zenica and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is P2078.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, P1988, is a document that the Judges have seen on several occasions. The date is quite important. It's April 20th, 1993, four days after Ahmici, when this document was signed between the BH Army and the HVO in the presence of the international community, General Morillon, extremely well known, and Ambassador Thebault, representing the European community. Now, I would like to know whether at the time you knew of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, on the 21st or 22nd, I already knew -- or, rather, there was this meeting in Vitez where they elaborated this actual document, in operational terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that on the 21st or the 22nd, you were aware of the document. When looking at paragraph 1 in this document, it seems that the international community is recognising the fact that the military HVO exists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was reality as of April 1992. If this was the beginning of recognition, in the sense of an official document, then maybe that might be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were not present on April 20th, when the negotiations occurred. But normally generals have a staff with them and legal advisers, and when they -- of course, General Morillon might not have studied law, but here we have the word "legal" in this text in item 1. You were a member of the HVO at the time, so did you feel that you belonged to a legal army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, since we went back to this Zenica agreement of the 20th of April, if you still have it in front of you, and it was P1988, let's take a look at point 3 of the document together. It says that: "A joint operations centre of Vitez was established at the level of the 3rd Corps of the BH Army and the HVO of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia as the beginning of the establishment of a joint command which will be finally established in the coming days." Now, was that the reason for the meeting in Vitez, General?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for the meeting in Vitez was a follow-up from the meetings in Vitez and Zenica. That's how I understood it, it was a continuation of those previous meetings. So apart from this meeting and this joint command, we had problems linked to the conflicts in the field, in the territory. But I don't think the meeting was convened to solve the joint command question, but it was to resolve the problems we were facing in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that later on when we come to Central Bosnia, Ahmici, and April 1993, those documents. But now let's look at the next document, which is P2078, 2078, 2078, that's right, which is a joint statement by Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, signed in Zagreb in the early hours of the 25th of April, 1993. And in point 3, it says that the BH Army and the HVO are legal units on a footing of equality and that a joint command of those forces should be established, composed of the representatives of both staffs." And the document refers to attachment 1, so let's take a look at that attachment 1 together, which is the next document. It is P2091, supplement 1, and this is a military supplement co-signed by Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic, and it says here as follows: "The BH Army and the HVO shall keep their separate identities and organisation of the command." Then point 2 says that they shall form a joint command which is going to be responsible for control of operations in the military districts. And then point 3 says the joint command shall consist of two supreme commanders, General Halilovic and General Petkovic, who shall meet on a regular basis, et cetera, et cetera. We don't need to read the rest. Tell us, please, General, to the best of your recollections, was that how it was? Did the BH Army and HVO need to continue as separate identities and then have a joint command which would co-ordinate their activities?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. My apologies for my voice. I seem to have a bit of a frog in my voice today. Your Honour, I know the witness has already answered, but I did want to object, in terms of time again, in terms of the question just now, "was it that way?" Does that mean is that what the document says, which we can all see what the documents say, or is that the way things were in reality? So at present, we don't know what exactly that means when the question is "was it that way?" I agree the document says that, but that doesn't really assist us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never ask the witnesses whether it says something in a document, because we can all read what a document says. My intention was to ask the witness whether that was how things happened in reality; that is to say, that the BH Army and the HVO kept their separate identities while attempting to establish a joint command which would co-ordinate their activities or, in other words, whether attempts were made to implement what was recorded in this document. I apologise if I wasn't sufficiently clear, but I think that the witness has already answered, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, as you know, the Prosecutor may have a frog in his throat, and to avoid that because he could just lose air and be unable to breathe, so do ask your questions in a classical fashion. As to the last document, you can see there's paragraph 3 that says that this joint command must be located or established in Travnik. The witness knows Travnik. Why don't you just ask him whether something happened in Travnik? He will say, Yes, or he will say, No, and so on, and then you could ask him whether he saw this document and whether the document was implemented, and he can answer, Yes, No. This way, you avoid objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that as Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic, I have the right to structure my examination-in-chief. So at present I'm not asking the witness about the joint command and its make-up, because if you look at the binder, this is going to be one of the next sections that we're going to address with respect to the system applied. But my intentions at present are to look at the HVO as a legal army. Now, since I was prevented from saying what my case was, given the documents, you're going to have to find your own way among these documents, but for the moment I am putting these documents to the witness exclusively from the standpoints of the HVO as a legal army and the HVO as a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, if there are other exceptionally interesting things in these documents, I'm not dealing with that now. So I'll be showing these documents again -- I'll come back to them when I deal with other issues of my examination-in-chief, but I would like to assure you that I'm going to cover all the topics, and not only the ones that the Petkovic Defence deems to be significant, but those that the Trial Chamber is interested in as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now, Witness, General, would you focus on the next document, which is 4D1611. There's something wrong with the channels. As I was saying, this was an order from Alija Izetbegovic, dated June 1993, ordering immediate cessation to all hostilities between the BH Army units and the HVO units. And in item 2, it says for the implementation of this order, the following persons shall be responsible: The commander of the BH Army, Rasim Delic, and commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, Milivoj Petkovic. Tell us, please, General, as a professional soldier yourself, here the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is he issuing an order here to the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the order relates to both the components of the army and to both individuals, both Delic and Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, the next document is 1D26644 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, allow me to return to this document, because if my memory serves me right, this is the first document we can see drafted in this way. It is entitled "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So far, nothing to say about it. But then we can see or read "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, HV," so one could be tempted to think that this is a document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "HVO," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could believe that this is a 100 per cent HVO document, but apparently it is signed by Izetbegovic, although we can't see or find any signature in the B/C/S document. This being said, if this is an authentic document, the president of the Presidency signed a document which was stamped as "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna/HVO." Unless Mr. Izetbegovic was not able to read or had no education at all, if he signed this document, that meant that, in his view, the HVO existed as such. What do you think? When you see this document signed by Mr. Izetbegovic, whilst it is a 100 per cent HVO document, what is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The heading here was the right one that was used from the first day, the HVO Croatian people, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, then the operative zone or whatever. So most of the documents had this same heading like a template. Now, I don't believe that Alija Izetbegovic signed this document in this form, but I do believe that it was conveyed to the HVO units or to the people whom it concerned in this particular form. Now, whether the signature is original or not or whether an original document was signed or not wasn't relevant at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate - the Defence will tell me if I'm wrong - but this is the first time I see an HVO document -- whilst we have 8.600 documents already, this is the first document in which mention is made of Izetbegovic as the signatory of Herceg-Bosna documents. There may be others, but this is the first one I see. However, you, yourself, said that this document is not signed by Izetbegovic, everybody can see that, but when you were in service did you receive this documents, because I see it is addressed to all the operative zones? Were you made aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been certainly in the Central Bosnia Operations Zone. Each document reached the operational zone. Whether it was distributed lower down the chain of command, that's something I could not comment upon, but it could not have been distributed lower down except in this form as we see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are four essential items in this document. The first one is cessation of hostilities. Item 2, appointment of Delic and Petkovic. Third item, the role played by the UNPROFOR. As to the fourth item, I can see it is that the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was to be a three-member presidency, is unanimous; in other words, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina agreed with the entire above text. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of timing, this came about after the Kiseljak meeting which I attended, in which I did take part, and it was then that we learned that Delic became commander instead of Sefer, I mean commander of the BiH Army. After that meeting, well, I simply -- the question is not specific enough for me to give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I highlighted the fact that there were four items in my question, and I return to the fourth item because it's always been said that Izetbegovic was the only one to rule or ruled alone; however, here we can see that he acted as president of the Presidency because it is written that the Presidency agreed with the text. You were on the ground. You may not have noticed all this, but I'm rather surprised to hear you say that this document was sent to the operative zone, and I wanted to know whether you read it. And you seem to say that you were not aware of it, so I'm rather puzzled, because this is such an important document that it's rather extraordinary that you -- you were on the ground. You were not made aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operations zone, the document arrived to it because there were technical prerequisites for it to be received at the operations zone. Very often, those technical requirements were not present at the lower units. The question is whether I saw that document at the time and studied it. Well, when you asked me whether it referred specifically to Petkovic, I answered, Yes. As for whether I saw that document, personally, is that the gist of your question, whether I did see it at the time? Nothing -- it would not strike me as strange for me to have seen it. I can confirm that I saw it at the Military District of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But wouldn't you have thought it strange that an HVO document was signed by Izetbegovic? I mean, this is really something out of the ordinary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could not have reached us in any other way as a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: General, Witness, I did not quite understand your last answer. I could imagine that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina takes a decision, which is put on paper, signed by the president of the Presidency, and then sent to the addressees, including the command of the HVO. You said the document could not have reached you in any other way than under the letterhead of the HVO. Is my -- why is my hypothesis, in your view, completely wrong? Why is it completely excluded that such an order be forwarded to the operations zone on the letterhead of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no technical capacities for the document to be received at the operations zone. It could have been brought by Sefer or Delic, or somebody of his personnel, in the form as it was created in Sarajevo, or, alternatively, it had to come from the Main Staff. There were no technical possibilities for the document to get there. That was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm still trying to understand, if you allow. Are you saying that while the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had authority over the HVO, it had only the possibility of addressing whom? You seem to say the Supreme Command, but not the operations zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Let me reiterate. The technical means -- for instance, on the 10th of that month, the APC of the British peacekeepers drove me around that area because there was no other way to go around on the 10th of June, so there were no technical means for that document, dated later, but in the way that I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In what technical -- on what technical way did the substance of the document reach you or reach the operations zone; by telephone, by telex, by fax, by satellite communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Maybe a combination of what you listed. There were no mobile phones at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And a last technical question. The document says the decision was taken in full composition, yes, so it appears that the Croat member of the Presidency also agreed to this. Do you know whether this is true? Do you have any other source that confirms that the Croat member of the Presidency also took part in this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not have such information, but I knew that there were two Croatian representatives or, rather, representatives of the Croatian people there in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott had been on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Mr. Scott. Witness, through the questions put by my fellow Judge, I think I understand what happened. On the 13th of June, in Geneva, Mr. Izetbegovic agreed to the four points we have here. Somebody from Geneva, from the Presidency, passed that on to the headquarters in Mostar, and at the Mostar headquarters this order was sent to the operational zones, itemising the four points that were communicated by telephone or by fax. Instead of signing "General Petkovic, Headquarters Commander," it was signed by the president of the Presidency, which would explain why the document is in this form. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that was the only reasonable solution. It had to arrive to the operations zone from Mostar because there was no other way, except hand delivery, for it to have been received from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott might shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me again, Your Honour. Your Honour, thank you. Mr. President, you just did, and that's the point that I was hoping to clarify. I think the mystery is largely assisted -- or answering the mystery is largely assisted, in addition to your comments, Judge Antonetti, by the subject reference. "Delivery of the text of," it's not an order from Izetbegovic. Someone, as you said in the HVO, is apparently transmitting what they've been told as something that Izetbegovic said, and it's not an order to the HVO. It is apparently Izetbegovic saying, "I ordered the cessation of hostilities between the ABiH and the HVO." So I think, Your Honour, you've noticed the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was ready to clarify this matter, but this is no longer necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's expound on this. When you say the paper could not have reached you, and you mentioned you were in UNPROFOR vehicles - we are talking about the 14th of June, 1993 - did Travnik fall into the hands of the BiH Army by that time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, in June 1993 was there conflict in other parts of Central Bosnia between BiH Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This was the most intense fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's take a look at the next document, 1D2664, which is minutes of a session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 29th of June, 1993. I'm interested in the discussion on whether the commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Army of BiH, Rasim Delic, can be a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina or not. And let me focus on two parts of this transcript. General, please listen to me. On page 1, it reads: "We recognise the HVO as a constituent part of the armed forces." And then discussion is held on whether Rasim Delic, as commander of one of the components of the armed forces, could be a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And later on, on page 8 in both versions, B/C/S and English, it reads as follows -- Alija Izetbegovic said: "For us, Mr. Delic is a member of the Presidency until it's proven differently or otherwise." And Mile Akmadzic responds, and Mile Akmadzic who was a Croat in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, says: "Please state for me. In my opinion, Mr. Delic is not part of the Presidency unless Mr. Petkovic joins him there." In your opinion, General, pursuant to your -- to the documents that you've seen so far and in your opinion, if the leading people of the armies that defend Bosnia-Herzegovina are supposed to be part of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your opinion, should members be chosen from the BiH Army and HVO or as Mr. Izetbegovic was right, saying that only Mr. Delic would have been there?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, neither of them should have been members. Attend meetings, yes, but it is blasphemous for me -- for them to be members of the Presidency. Secondly, around that time, although we tried to reach agreements, at the time the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army exerted the most intense pressure against the HVO units, and most of the Croatians suffering during the war occurred around that time. And for Delic to be a member of the Presidency while they were carrying out such policies on the field, well --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There was no way for Delic to be a member of the Presidency, but if he was there, my opinion is that he should not have been there without General Petkovic also in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next document, 4D1300. This is an agreement on the structure of the Joint Staff of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 26th of March, 1994. It was signed by Rasim Delic and Ante Roso. And it stated, among other things, that the Joint Staff is going to comprise of ten members, five from each side. And in item 3, it's stated that the erstwhile manners of commanding BiH Army and HVO is continued and maintained during the transitional period until federal army mechanisms are set up. General, in spring-time 1994 were you familiar with the establishment of such joint Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This was after the Washington Agreement, when the fighting stopped, and the Washington Agreement is being operationalised. And I knew about this Joint Staff and Command. Fikret Muslimovic, for instance, one month after fighting, spent a night at the Vitez headquarters, in the command building at Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fikret Muslimovic was a high-ranking officer in the Security Administration of BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I shouldn't have mentioned his name, but, in essence, he was the most competent person, after Delic, in the army. But that's only my assessment. I knew him from our JNA days in Doboj. Fikret Muslimovic was assistant to Aca Vasiljevic. The area of responsibility was Drava to the Adriatic and from Drina to the Una Rivers. They were very effective. Fikret Muslimovic was a very capable person.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now the last document in this section is 4D826 that I'd like to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me return to the previous document. It's several pages long, so by the time I've reached the end, I'll let Ms. Alaburic put her questions about the document. This is the 207th meeting of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Page 21, Izetbegovic is answering Boras, a Croat, and Izetbegovic mentions the fact that nothing has been signed in Lisbon, that the negotiations have been interrupted. He says that Sarajevo is not destroyed by the Presidency or by the negotiations, but by those firing from the hills. So now he has the Serbs in mind. But then he says, They destroyed the city, and then he mentions Mostar. He says now Mostar has been destroyed from two sides, from both sides. How do you interpret the last sentence, when he said, And now -- so now that is at the date of the meeting, 29th of June, 1993. So when he said, Now Mostar has been destroyed from two sides, what did he mean? Did he mean the Muslim and the Croat sides, or the Croat side and the Serb side? How do you interpret this sentence by Mr. Izetbegovic, who said that, I quote: "Now Mostar has been destroyed from two sides"? What did he mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He probably meant the Serb and Croatian side, because Mostar was destroyed until June 1992 by the Serbs. They were destroying it until then. And then in the war between the TO and HVO, they were destroyed by both sides, so that in fact three sides were destroying it. But probably Mr. Izetbegovic meant the Serbs and the Croats in this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that Mr. Izetbegovic meant the Serb and the Croat sides. Well, then in June, in other words, back in June 1993, the Serbs were still firing on Mostar; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From time to time, yes, they targeted it, but not in support of the fighting, just a sporadic gun-shot here and there. But the heavy shelling in Mostar -- well, heavy shells were falling on Mostar at that time, and the only people that could have had shells of that calibre were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen to my question carefully and think it through before you answer it. You've just said that every now and then the Serbs would fire on Mostar. Let us imagine a victim that was hit by shrapnel. It's just a hypothesis. How can you ascertain that the shrapnel originates from the HVO or from the Serbs? Do you have a military answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had been there, I would know by the trajectory or the type of explosion, if I was there. If I were to see the crater, I would know, once again, the direction the shell came from. But the general public couldn't have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just briefly on this document, and then we can take the break. And it's 4D826, the next document that I'd like us to look at, which is a Law on Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we're only interested in one article there, and it is Article 37, para 2, where it says: "The Army of the Federation is composed of units of the BH Army and the Croatian Defence Council, inclusive of the corps level and military district, made up of peacetime and wartime components." Now, as defined here, was the HVO entirely a component part of the Army of the BH Federation?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is the "Official Gazette" dating back to 1996, so there's no dilemmas on that score. The Army of the Federation was made up of two components, and at that point in time they had a joint staff, and most of the activities they waged were the activities of a single army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I think we can take the break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's move on to the next area. And in order to do that, look at P280, which is an order jointly signed by Mate Boban and General Roso, dated the 27th of June, 1992. And for commander of the HVO Staff of Central Bosnia, as it was already, Tihomir Blaskic is being appointed to the post, and he's being given various authorisations, as it says here, for the full articulation of all combat operations in Central Bosnia. On the basis of this order, General -- well, he wasn't general at the time, but, anyway, Colonel Blaskic, Tihomir Blaskic, also appointed and relieved of duty commanders of military units. Tell us now, please, General, at that time did you know whether the commanders of the other operative zones in the HVO had the same remit and authorisations?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when this document -- whether they did when this document was actually written, but it was logical that Tihomir Blaskic did have those authorisations linked to the territory he was in command of and the people he knew, as this was a little separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said because of the isolation of the territory, because the territory was isolated. The isolation of the territory of Herceg-Bosna; is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He did, he said so, but the transcript was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All I can do, of course, is respond to what's either translated orally or in writing, Your Honour, and I did not hear the witness say that at all. I also did not -- there's nothing on the face of the document that says anything about it being involving the appointment or removal of commanders, and there again I'm sorry to say it, because I have great respect of Ms. Alaburic as a fine colleague, but it's again suggesting answers to the witness, and the document -- the interpretation of the document and where the document, on its face, says nothing of the sort. All the document says is "is fully responsible for full articulation." It says nothing about how that relates to the appointment or dismissal of other commanders. That was completely injected by Ms. Alaburic, and it's not appropriate, Your Honour, and I'm going to object. I do object.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if after four years we have to discuss such a banal matter as the appointment and dismissal of duties that Tihomir Blaskic conducted in Central Bosnia, then I don't know what it is that we've been doing for all this time here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But tell me, to the best of your knowledge, General, did Tihomir Blaskic, as the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, appoint and relieve of duty military commanders in that operative zone?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In point 2 of this document, it says "appoints commanders of the HVO in Central Bosnia," so as far as I'm concerned that's clear. And in practice, yes, he did appoint commanders in Central Bosnia. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if Mr. Scott wishes to apologise, I accept his apology in advance. Let's now look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I still submit that the document does not say what counsel has indicated it does. It's unfortunate, but I understand that she may wish that's what it says, but the document doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, so we have a document in front of us appointing Mr. Blaskic as the main commander of the staff of the HVO in Central Bosnia. This is a document signed by Mr. Boban. But the thing that puzzles me is this: We can also see Mr. Roso, who was then the Chief of Staff, who also signed the document. You were there. You may know. Does this mean that Mr. Mate Boban appointed the main officials within the HVO Command and within the operative zone, and it happened that he appointed them based on a document drafted by the headquarters that prepared this order for appointment, as you can see, because you can see the number, 396, and thereafter Boban signed? But since the document was prepared by the Main Staff, it was also signed by the head of the Main Staff; is that so? Is that the reason why we can see that Mr. Roso intervened in the appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is correct is that the proposals or, rather, appointments went from Boban -- from the Main Staff to Boban. Now, why Roso's signature is here, I really don't know. Only Boban's signature was enough, but you couldn't have just Roso's signature. So why the two are there, I don't know. But Mate Boban's signature gave legitimacy to the whole affair because it was the major unit in the HVO of the operative zone or, rather, the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the same line, Witness, on the top left hand of the document we read "Main Staff," so the origin of the document is not at the Presidency, it appears, but at the Main Staff. Is it possible that the chief of the Main Staff, General Roso, drafts this as a proposal, perhaps after telephone conversation, then sends it with his signature to Mate Boban, and Mate Boban signs to sanctify the document? Could it have happened like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Boban signed first, and then since it goes up the chain of command -- through the chain of command and communications from the Main Staff towards the operative zone, and I see nothing contentious there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't implying anything contentious. I'm just trying to find out the truth. Later on, we will see what is of importance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are just my introductory remarks about Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now moving on to Ahmici on the 16th of April and a few events before that, but let's look at the next document, which is P661, and it is the appointment of the commanders of operations zones which, on the 28th of October, 1992, was effected by the president of the HZ-HB, Mate Boban. And here, under item 3, we see that he appointed for commander of the operative zone Tihomir Blaskic. Now, my question to you, General, is this: If you remember, roughly when was it that the HVO was organised in such a way as to establish operations zones?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was roughly this time, because the same unit and the same commands were called differently before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document now, which is P554. This is an order from Tihomir Blaskic on the organisation of units in the Central Bosnia Operations Zone. Tell us, please, General, were you aware of this order at that time? Did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It was -- I initiated this because it was an enormous zone, and in order to facilitate command I proposed that four operative zones or tactical groups within operative zones be established. And geographically, they ran along Vrabac-Lasva, and emerging on to Zenica, then the valley of Bosna, Zepce, and that area over there, and then Lepenica, that general area, so tactically or operationally it was justified to establish zones and the tactical groups. And there were about six municipalities to one tactical group. I was the commander of one of those, one of those tactical groups from Jajce to Zenica inclusive, along with my regular duties, that is, as deputy commander of the operative zone or military district of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, when you say you were at the head of a tactical group, and you told us which one, is it the one that is stipulated in item 1(b)?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, although the Dobratici municipality, or Pogradje, in comprising Kotor Varos municipality and Skender Vakuf municipality, isn't mentioned here, so that was that sixth area or entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Let's look at the next document, which is P658.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to know whether, as far as this last document is concerned, in the chain of command we have: Mate Boban as president, being number 1, then we have the commander of the HVO, i.e., General Petkovic here, then number 3 would be the commander of the operative zone, Tihomir Blaskic, and then in your own operative zone the commander of the tactical group, i.e., you, and then below you the commanders of brigades within this tactical group? Does this represent the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to draw your attention to the title of the post of Milivoj Petkovic on page 44, line 13 -- or I correct myself, line 12. It is defined as commander of the HVO, and the function was entitled "Chief of the Main Staff." It is important, for the Defence case of General Petkovic, to refer to him as chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's take a look at the next document, P658.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you might be able to shed some light on this. Can you tell us what difference you make, yourself, between the commander of the HVO and head of the Main Staff? Are these two different positions? If so, who is in command of the HVO? And if not, what can you say about this? Because Ms. Alaburic seems to make a difference between these two, and I would like to know exactly how things stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over different time-periods, there was the commander of the HVO and the Chief of Staff or chief of the Main Staff. However, for the most part, for most of the duration and the existence of that, we had the chief of the Main Staff who was the link between the president and units, in general. So if there was no appointed commander of the HVO, then the chief of the Main Staff, for the most part, held command role, except if it was otherwise in certain areas. But I'm telling you this from my position, how I understood the chain of command. So that would be Blaskic, Petkovic, or Roso, whoever was chief of the Main Staff, and at the top Mate Boban in all his functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 7th of October, 1992 - that's the date of the document - who was the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the operations zone or the corps, it was Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was the HVO military commander. I want to know who commanded the military HVO, the one who was in command of all the operative zones. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The term "HVO" entails political, military, and other dimensions. But in respect of the unit of the HVO, the military wing of the HVO, Blaskic was the commander, but he was not the commander to other elements of life and authorities in the area of his responsibility, in military terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, because I'm totally lost now. I've been now involved 150 per cent of my time in this case for four years, and now I'm discovering something totally new. Maybe it was poorly translated; I don't know. But you just said, because I did ask you this: Back in October, who was the HVO commander? And I specified my question. I said I want to know who was in command of all the various operative zones. And your answer is that, in your view, it was Blaskic, so now I fail to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're discussing a document which discusses tactical groups within the corps or operational zone, then Blaskic was the commander of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that. He was the commander of the HVO in the operative zone. There, I agree with you. But I wanted to know who was the HVO commander of all the operative zones, of all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mate Boban, Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now this is a very exact answer. You are telling me that the HVO commander was Mate Boban. Then there's a chief of Main Staff, and that was General Petkovic. And then there are operative zone commanders, so in Central Bosnia it was Blaskic. And then you have commanders of tactical groups, and you were one of them for the 2nd Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Lozancic was in Zepce, and that tactical group comprised Zepce, Zavidovici, Teslic, Maglaj. In Lepenica, there was Rajic, and it comprised Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, Vares, and Kakanj. And the 4th Operations Group, Bugojno, Kupres, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Jablanica, and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I may be slow of understanding, perhaps, dimwitted, perhaps, but I still am not quite clear on this, because at one point the Presiding Judge put to you a line of command which went: Boban, Chief of Staff, chiefs of operations zones; Blaskic was the chief of an operations zone.
