You said above him there was Boban. But according to the line of command previously established, above him was Petkovic was the chief of the General Staff. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Boban was the supreme commander, and the Main Staff supports and works for him. The chief of the Main Staff carries out the orders, the desires, of Boban, and chief of the Main Staff relays to us, at the operations zone, in the form of orders what we're supposed to do. So you asked of me to precise [as interpreted] the line of command as per definition, but I am telling you how I understood it to be. I knew that my immediate superior was Blaskic. I was his deputy, and I knew that he -- his commander or person who he reports to and receives orders from was the chief of the Main Staff, and sometimes there was direct link to Boban. That was the practice in use throughout that time, except for a time when the chief of the Main Staff was number 3 in the military hierarchy of the HVO, because there was the commander, then the deputy commander, and then the chief of the Main Staff, but that was for a relatively brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have clarified my question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no supplementary questions to your description. I just wanted to intervene as to the title of the function. Let's take a look at the next document, P658. This is a consolidated report for the 26th October 1992. General, in respect of the Jajce theory, it is stated that the Chetniks are attacking with everything they have and firing between 25 and 30 hundred [as interpreted] projectiles a day, so that everything is burning. Tell us, General, since we have seen fierce discussions in this courtroom whether Serbs and Croats did fight each other at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, please tell us, did you conduct any combat against the Serbs, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina Serbs, in 1992 and after that date?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this item is a wound still fresh in me. I've invested quite a lot of my efforts into the defence of Jajce. This refers to a period prior to Jajce's fall. And as far as the Serbian forces throughout 1992 and 1993, until June 1993, the only enemy out there was the VRS, the Army of the Republika Srpska. And when we lost in Central Bosnia, direct contact with the VRS, the only enemy was the ABiH or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In our -- Jajce front-line was 100 kilometres' long because it was separate from the Lasva Valley front-line, and they had constant fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, when you say that in Central Bosnia you lost contact with the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, was that the time when the Croatian enclave was created in Central Bosnia, or did you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993? I said throughout 1992 and 1993, inclusive with June. At that time, during that period, the only enemy was the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 6 of this report, which refers to Travnik, it is stated on the basis -- well, that part of the report refers to Central Bosnia. It is a report by Tihomir Blaskic, and it states: "On the basis of the order of the supreme commander, number 396, dated 27th of June, 1992: 2. I reorganised the entire staff and relieved members of the staff, and appointed Colonel Filip Filipovic as commander." Just one note before I ask you a question. General, the document that is being referred to is the document that we discussed, the P280 document, so that was the document on the basis of which Tihomir Blaskic appointed and relieved of duties commanders. Could you please tell us, General, was that the time when you were appointed the commander of the brigade in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the period when the commander of the Travnik Brigade was killed by Muslim forces, and this brigade was partly in disarray. And on top of my other duties, I took, pursuant to this command, over the command of that brigade, the Travnik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, General, who was at the head of the Muslim forces in Travnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Alpha and Omega, there was Colonel Alagic, Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us whether and how did you co-operate with Colonel Alagic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We co-operated in the first year of the conflict. The second year of the war, we fought intense battles. And after the -- in the third year, after the Washington Agreement, we co-operated again. I must say that Mehmed Alagic was a fair both ally and opponent in all respects. He was a very difficult negotiator, but when you've reached an agreement with him, you could be sure that the agreement will be implemented.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, may we have your comments to this statement about the good co-operation between Filipovic and Alagic? And it was an international observer in BH who presented this view.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This observation is highly technical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'd just like to correct the transcript on page 8 [as interpreted]. The question that I quoted relates to Colonel Filipovic, not Colonel Alagic. So "Colonel Filipovic" it should read, page 51, line 8. The question was: "Do you know what became of Colonel Filipovic?" Now, your comments about this statement that you cooperated well?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: A professional view, realistic from those times. Perhaps it's a little exaggerated to say that I let it be known that I was being supported by my superiors. I always had very proper co-operation with Blaskic, and I don't really know what that referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you explain to us, General, about this departure of yours to another location, that final part of the portion I read out? What would that refer to, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my departure from Travnik, probably. I went to the commission that we already mentioned, as a member of the commission, as a member of the joint command, so there should be no insinuations as to why I left. It was quite logical that I should do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at document 4D1700, which is an order for defence of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia compiled by Tihomir Blaskic. Tell us, please, General, are you familiar with this document? Did you know about it before?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I took part in its writing, because it was a consolidated document for a given period and for a given time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the document, there is no date, General. So judging by the contents, could you give us a date for the document, when it was written?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the names of the units, when they were established and when they appeared, like the 2nd Zenica, and the Jure Francetic Brigade, and the Travnik Brigade, this was the time -- well, I would say it was mid-March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In several places in this document, for example, in item 2 and item 5(1), Tihomir Blaskic plans the organisation of Central Bosnia's defence in co-operation with the BH Army units. My question to you is this, General: Did you plan the defence of the territory which came under your responsibility with respect to defence preparations and combat? Did you plan to co-operate with the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We co-operated with the BH Army throughout this time and jointly held the defence lines, so that there's no question that co-operation was envisaged with the BH Army units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D389, which is an order from the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, Milivoj Petkovic, dated December 1992. And in the introduction of this order, General, it says that interception of Chetnik conversations -- by tapping into Chetnik conversations, the HVO learnt that the Army of Republika Srpska considers that there was very little to go, allegedly, to the end of the war, and that over the next five or six days it would attempt to undertake some particular action. Now, at that point in time, General, that is to say, at the end of December 1992, for the territory on which you were active in the defence, were you threatened by the Army of Republika Srpska in any way? Was it a threat and danger to you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It was a threat throughout in the war, and this is probably linked to the Christmas holiday preparations. I am speculating here, but looking at the date, I assume that we were to hold strong there, but the Chetnik -- the defence lines facing the Chetniks was -- they were active all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at item 5 of this order, where combat readiness is to be raised, and it says: "In executing this order, achieve full co-ordination with the BH Army units." May we have your comments, General, to that item of this order by the general?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you want me to comment. It was understood, implied. And I'd like to emphasise once again that full co-ordination is stressed once again with the BH Army, not to forget the allies or the neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at another document. It is 4D830. I am just interested in the last portion of that document, to be found on the last page. It's very short, General, but this is what it says. This is a report from the chief of the Main Staff for 1992, and then it says: "The HVO forces, in addition to the many problems and difficulties, have successfully under their control 70 per cent of free territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, my question to you, General, is this: To the best of your recollections, roughly speaking, what portion of the front-line facing Republika Srpska were held by the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, more than half. I would have to measure the distance on a map, but I think that this piece of information here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next sentence reads: "By organising its own armed forces in the territory of HZ-HB, the Croatian people defended themselves and the majority of the Muslims." My question to you, General, is this: When you were defending Bosnia-Herzegovina in Central Bosnia, were you just defending the Croatian people or not?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said I defended myself, my family, the local community, the broader community, and the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in defending this particular territory and area, I was, in fact, defending everybody in the area, including the Serbs and the Muslims. And in the first two or three months of the war, it is true that we managed to defend everyone, but as of June the Territorial Defence or the BH Army carried its part of the burden and responsibility, and it was only as of June 1992, on a footing of equality, was it able to fight at the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, in the area that you were in, Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik and Vitez, that general area, roughly speaking, ratios and proportions between the Croatian and Muslim population, was there a majority ethnic group in the territory, more than --

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the Lasva Valley, there were slightly more Muslims, but generally speaking, it was a 50:50 ratio.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, in the Lasva River Valley, did refugees begin coming into the area?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The refugees started coming in from the very first days, but the majority came in May and June and later on in the autumn, because the Serbs would send in the Muslims and some Croats, 4 to 5 per cent, but in their masses, in large quantities, thousands of people coming in, coming down from the Serb lines and crossing over on to our side, that happened, too, and those refugees needed help and assistance in those first days because they were a pitiful group.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What year are you referring to, General?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that very few Croats were coming in, 4 to 5 per cent. Now, tell us, please, if you can, whether the Croats from these areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, did they go to some other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina or to some other countries?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite logically, from that western area of Republika Srpska or, rather, the area under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, it was easier for them to ship the Croats across the river. That's how I understood it, across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, roughly speaking, how many refugees there were until the end of 1992, who arrived in the Lasva River Valley? What figure would that be?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Tens of thousands of people. The lowest figure that I can quote is 20.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And percentage-wise, as you told us, were these wholly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something, General, about the first half of 1992 and the arrival of soldiers into the Lasva River Valley? Did they come into the area? Where did they come from? What ethnicity did they belong to, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said that they accepted me as commander in the Lasva River Valley. I was accepted as commander by one and all with respect to my activities and so forth. But the first people to arrive were foreigners, El Mujahid later on, but a negligible number of them. Anyway, sometime at the beginning of May, 50 buses arrived of a unit that had been established. The 1st Krajina Brigade, that's what it was called at the time, and it was put up at the barracks in Travnik. Up until then, I had struck -- I had a fair balance between the BH Army and the number of Muslims, but with the arrival of refugees and with the arrival of others coming into the area, this balance was upset in Travnik, in that general area. And at first, I was happy to reinforce my own forces facing the enemy. However, coupled with the arrival of the refugees, who had nothing and needed everything, and were put up in the area, such as the Croatian religious sites, the Croatian shrines, churches, the school building and so on, all these buildings and facilities that could take in large numbers of people --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. Before the next question, could I just ask for assistance to get a date, because the only thing that's been referenced so far was --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, yes, that's why I interrupted you. You've been talking for quite some time, but we've lost our bearings in terms of time. Now, everything you've just described to us, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The beginning of the war, that is to say, the first couple of months of 1992 or, rather, April, May, and June of that year. And the refugees continued to pour in in the autumn, and they culminated with the arrival of all -- the whole of Jajce and Pogra [phoen] until the beginning of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Krajina Brigade, and you said that its members arrived in busloads, 50 buses. And if my calculations are correct, that would make it about 2.000 soldiers. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That would be the maximum number. Including equipment and everything else, the figure would be less, around 1500. And I'd like to mention that they arrived from the Republika Hrvatska -- Croatia area, from the Republic of Croatia. And I found nothing bad in terms of defence during that first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a time-frame for the arrival of the Krajina Brigade, once again?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It was about the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, what ethnicity were the soldiers of the Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They were exclusively Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, if, from the standpoint of the territorial army or the manoeuvre army, you were to compare your own HVO and this Krajina Brigade, what could you tell us about the HVO and about the Krajina Brigade in those terms?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I have the Home Guards, who were put up in their own homes, who lived at home. And when the time came for them to go up to the front-line, then I would have about 20 per cent of my men up at the front-lines, but I did not have any manoeuvre units able to intervene in any way. The intervention platoons were only to arrive later. And the Krajina Brigade, since it was a pure -- they were pure soldiers, they were put up in the barracks, and it was a manoeuvre unit and the only unit of that kind able to carry out manoeuvres in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, now you've just said that the intervention platoons arrived later on. Did those intervention platoons come from outside Central Bosnia or did you establish those intervention platoons from your own forces, your own men?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, exclusively made up of my own men. When the need arose, that's when that unit was established, because you needed a soldier that you could command and send out in manoeuvres, and not only soldiers up at the front-lines in the trenches. You needed someone to carry out the manoeuvring actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, this Krajina Brigade, once it reached the Lasva River Valley, did it join up with the HVO or the BH Army, or was it perhaps a sort of independent, autonomous force in the area?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At first -- or, rather, up until the arrival of Alagic and Cuskic -- well, they did not arrive with them. It was, well, still unidentified, or, rather, it conducted training and was being established. But once we had the firm chain of command for the BH Army, it became exclusively a component part of the Territorial Defence or, rather, the BH Army. I use both terms because I don't know the date exactly when the Territorial Defence became the BH Army or was divided into the Territorial Defence and the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, General, the hard-line corps in the Army of BiH. Could you please explain what was that about?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to that area in the Lasva River Valley, I had four municipal crisis headquarters and some crisis headquarters which derived from the times of Yugoslavia, and in terms of division of authorities in those four municipalities, the president of the municipality would be a Muslim, the executive council president would be Croatian, the secretary for defence would be a Croat, a commander of the Territorial Defence would be a Muslim, so I encountered four commanders of the Territorial Defence staffs who were Muslims, which was a bit strange, in my opinion, but that was so. I co-operated with them, and as I said, I was accepted as a commander by all of them, and my orders were accepted by those on the front-line. And there was a point where I realised that all four of them have been removed from their duties, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before you continue, General, could you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: June 1992. In June 1992, there was a large number of Muslim officers who arrived to the Lasva River Valley area, and presidents of municipalities were changed. In Travnik, there used to be Tamburic, but he was replaced by Hodzic; in Novi Travnik, the commander was -- the name escapes me, but Lendo replaced him. And there was a change in the personnel, not only in terms of names but in terms of actions in the area of responsibility of the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was that change when the hard-lines came?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the change was that they no longer accepted me as commander, neither did they accept my suggestions, and if I had to change or do something, I would have to go down to commands for activities to be carried out as intended. They demonstrated their powers by moving forces and units from one settlement to another. There was a large number of such units established. The insignia in units and signs in the area changed. A large number of green flags cropped up suddenly. Simply, you could feel it. I could list you other occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I would like to ask a question of you, Mr. Filipovic, regarding page 60, line 9. You said that for commanders of the Territorial Defence staffs were Muslims and added "which was a bit strange, in my opinion." Would you be so kind as to explain why you thought this was strange, and to what degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the 1990 elections, in this area SDA and HDZ were the victors, and they combined their personnel to set up authorities. And if this was so, then, in my opinion, they should have mixed and combined the personnel and their cadres differently, more smartly. It could not function at any time in Bosnia and Herzegovina to have a monolithic structure. You had to be mindful of both Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. And to see four of them being Muslims, it was strange -- seemed strange to me because of the way I was brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. But you have spoken about several key roles, and there was some, I seem to recall, where they were all Croats. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Presidents of municipalities would be Muslims. Presidents of executive councils of those municipalities would be Croats. Secretaries for defence of municipalities would be Croats, and commanders of staffs of the Territorial Defence, meaning the army, would be Muslims. At first glance, it would seem to be a good mix, but when it came to defence it seemed strange to me that I had to co-operate with four commanders of Territorial Defence staffs who were all Muslims, and them being all Muslims was a bit strange to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic, for having interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, did you have any problems in co-operating with somebody just because they were Muslim? Was it important to you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not important. I did co-operate, and they did accept me. But for somebody being brought up in Bosnia, that person should be mindful of the three peoples in Bosnia at all times. For instance, when I would have a hay load on a cart, and there were some bronze rings around the horses that were drawing the cart, I would then silence the bells whenever I would drive through a Muslim village, being mindful of the sensitivities of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Those bronzes, you mean the bells?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the bells, but made of the same materials as church bells.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. We fully understand the example that you illustrated. Please do explain to the people who do not hail from the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I'm not sure whether they understand what you meant by silencing the bells whenever you passed through a Muslim village. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Because you may upset the inhabitants of that Muslim village. Out of respect towards people, out of understanding that this is a different community and that you had to adapt your own behaviour; as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine, General. Let's go back to the people who started arriving at the Lasva River Valley. Did something happen after the fall of Jajce? Did some other people come to the Lasva River Valley after that point?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The fiercest fighting up to that point in the Central Bosnia theatre was in Jajce. There were 100 kilometres of front-line there. I helped them through -- sending people through the Lasva River Valley through woods to get to Jajce, and when Jajce fell some 2.000 combatants, Croats, and 2.000 good fighters, Muslims, suddenly appeared in the area of Travnik, the only difference being that the Croats continued through to the Republic of Croatia and elsewhere in the world, whereas the Muslims remained in my area of operation. And that tipped the scales and the balance was lost, because automatically I knew that I was weaker by 4.000 men. While the balance was there, it was all fine, but now I was weaker by 4.000 good combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One question for you, General. We're still discussing 1992. Did you plan, in 1992, any attack on the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was in no position to plan or to attack BiH Army at any point in time, not because I was not irritated, but, first of all, I did not have the forces, and the result of such an attack would be a defeat, and both by the enemy against whom I maintained my defence lines, but also in the rear. So it was out of the question to conduct military activities, but what could be done was to prevent what was being done throughout that time, in terms of threats or jeopardy to the defence of those who are represented at the time throughout my life, and that would be the people of the Lasva River Valley and in the area of my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us whether, in 1993, the situation changed.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to note that what I discussed was the situation in the Lasva River Valley in the tactical group area. Problems were not similar in Zepce, Kiseljak, or Bugojno, in the other three tactical groups. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have to repeat your question [as interpreted] because you continued answering my previous question. My question was: As pertained to the River Lasva Valley, in terms of planning attacks against the BH Army, did anything change in 1993? Did you plan to attack the army then?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not change -- nothing changed until June 1993, when the only enemy left out there was the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in June 1993, General, did you start attacking the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm discussing a time where there could be no co-operation, no agreements made or negotiated -- negotiations conducted, except for the exchange of the dead and the wounded. This is the period I'm discussing. Up to that point, there was co-operation, negotiations, avoidance of conflicts, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if we had to define, of course, it's difficult to say because of the many dissidents [as interpreted] who were first to do something, but if we had to define who attacked whom and who captured certain areas, what would you say? Who went on the offensive? Who captures territory, the BiH Army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of the area or in terms of successes, the HVO did not achieve any successes, which means they did not attack. If anybody achieved successes, it was the BiH Army, and they attacked. You see, nowhere were those attacks of high intensity so that you could say a whole brigade is attacking to reach a certain position. Up to June 1993, those combat activities were of low intensity. There were skirmishes here and there, incidents here and there. You had to try to solve them or not. There was movement of and transport of population, people moved out of the area where they were threatened, and the accumulation of those low-intensity incidents provided you with an answer to the question who got the initiative and who was attacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, you said "transport of population." We are going to deal with that in great detail. General, please tell us, did you say "transport of the population," or did you say that people left the areas where there were combat activities going on? Please tell us. This formulation could be --

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where you got the transport. When the Serbs deliver 10, or 5.000 people, or 2.000, then we would transport them somewhere somehow. Maybe the question is unclear. In this document that I'm reading, do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, we're not dealing with documents. I'm trying to analyse what you said in the manner it was reflected in the transcript, and the transcript reflects something that you did not say, and this is what I'm trying to rectify. Let me be precise. Page 65, line 10, reference is being made of transport of population, and the witness mentioned that he never used the word "transport" of the population? We are going to deal with June -- it is line 10 in my screen. General, we are going to deal extensively with June 1993, so I'm going to stop here. If I understood you correctly, you never planned any offensive activities against the BiH Army. Did I get you loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive from Tihomir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier we had a document on the screen, 4D830. This is a document dated February 1993, but it's a report for the period from April 14, 1992, through December 31st, 1992. The document is signed by General Petkovic. I was looking at this document, and I focused on the brigades. I counted them all. There are 26 altogether. And according to this document, I noted that there were 45.000 troops in HVO units. It's written there are 955 professional soldiers, 85 officers, 91 NCOs, and 670 professional soldiers; this is the situation as described by General Petkovic. And I tried to break this down into 26 brigades, and as a ballpark figure we have about 2.000 soldiers for the brigade, we have 85 officers. Divided by 26, that gives me 2 to 3 professional officers per brigade, and about the same amount of NCOs. It seems that the HVO is made up of a hard core of about a thousand professional soldiers. The Prosecutor's case is that the HVO had a plan and the plan of the HVO was ethnic cleansing, so I'm wondering the following: I'm wondering whether in the framework of this plan, it was possible to carry out this plan with only a thousand professional soldiers, in terms of logistics. So you were on the field, on the ground, and all the witnesses we have are witnesses who were on the field, so I will put this question to you: When you were there -- and you had a high rank, so you may be able to answer my question. So I'd like to know the following: Given the number of units in the HVO, given the very low number of professional soldiers, officers, and NCOs, do you think that the HVO would have been able to carry out an all-out action against the Muslims and against the BH Army, given the number of troops that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a flagrant lack of professionals in the HVO units. In the Lasva Valley, I didn't have more than three or four professionals [as interpreted], where I had -- whereas I had 5.000 or 6.000 fighters. We had reserve officers from the Territorial Defence, but that, too, was few in number compared to the number of inhabitants and the proportionate number that should have been there. So there was a flagrant lack of people able to command and conduct operations. When you say "brigade," yes, it's true that we did call it a brigade, but that brigade was just able to hold its positions, to hold the defence lines. However, the Serbs weren't able to attack too much, either, and that was comforting because there was an extensive front-line. Otherwise, these units, which we referred to as brigades, they would have been vanquished very quickly, in military terms. So given these conditions, to plan attacks -- and if you planned an attack, you could just have an intervention platoon going into action, and that was only possible later on, at a later stage, once they were established, so it would be completely senseless and mad to do that. We had an HVO army only towards the end of 1994, an army in the sense of -- well, we called it the Guards Brigade, but in operational terms it was the strength of a battalion. I don't know whether that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we could correct the transcript straight away. Otherwise, the sentence doesn't read properly. On page 67, line 17, the witness said -- line 16, the sentence begins: "In the Lasva River Valley, I didn't have more than three or four soldiers," professionals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professional soldiers, yes, that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professional soldiers, and the witness has just made that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When answering my question, you say that it's only in 1994 that the HVO had a real army, not before. Now, let me be more specific in my question. We've seen a number of documents and plans where the HVO and the BH Army were facing the lines against the Serbs, so they were in position against the Serbs. So there were these front-lines, but the HVO and the BiH were deployed on the terrain also, not just on the front-line. Now, looking at these maps, since I don't have the breakdown of HVO on the front-line facing the Serbs, and HVO in the rear in Herceg-Bosna, able to launch actions against the BH Army, but as far as these HVO deployed in Herceg-Bosna but who were not on the front-line, I would like to know whether they would have been able to launch attacks against the BH Army in order to achieve the plan. Let me tell you that we had a witness sitting exactly where you are a few weeks ago, and he said that when you launch an attack, if you want to win, the ratio has to be 3:1, if you want to win. If you don't have this ratio, you just don't launch the attack. And this is my question: Given the troops that the HVO had - I'm talking about here HVO not on the front-line facing the Serbs - do you believe that you would have been able to win an attack against the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. We did not have a unit for us to attack the enemy, the Serbs. We didn't attack anywhere; not because we didn't want to, because we'd lost too much, but we weren't able to. In Travnik, on my family heritage, there was this Serb, and I'd like -- I wanted to have them expelled, but I wasn't able to. So when somebody is under attack, then a mountain is made out of a mole hill, and then you defend yourself not as an army but as an individual, if you make a mountain out of a mole hill. And I'm speaking about the in-depth territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So taking up again this formula, you said that when you are under attack, a mouse can become a lion. If you look at the conclusion in this document signed by General Petkovic, it looks as though the HVO forces were able to defend themselves. That's what he says. So as I understand it, you were able to defend yourself, but not able to attack. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said compared to the Serb forces, because the territory was very large and the Serbs didn't have the kind of army they wanted either, but with this deployment, and the level of equipment, and the establishment of units, we were successful in defending ourselves. That's the truth of it. But to attack, except for skirmishes or some smaller diversionary or sabotage action, we weren't able to attack, so we couldn't attack the enemy, the Serbs, and we especially couldn't attack on our territory in depth where, in terms of numbers and equipment and the number of professional soldiers we had, and other types of professionals, we were three or four times weaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we need a subject, verb, object here. So who do you mean by "in depth"? Who was in depth, as far as you were concerned, who you could perhaps attack, but that force was three or four times stronger? Who is that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the defence line, and the defence line was one or two kilometres. And I'm talking about the in-depth area where the population lived and where the soldiers were staying at home, in their own homes. Well, perhaps it's clear to me, but not to you. But when I say "in-depth," everything -- when I say "in-depth," I mean everything that isn't up at the front-line, the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So we have the defence line, the front-line. On one side are the Serbs, on the other side are the Croats and the Muslims; is that right? Is that how it was? Was that how I define the defence line and confrontation line properly?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, General, that the Croats and Muslims, together with -- were together, were in-depth, that side of the defence line? Were they together?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were together, and so was life in general, it was on that side of the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about the capabilities of the HVO of launching attacks, both vis-a-vis the Serbs and vis-a-vis the Muslim army, and you said that you were not capable of launching attacks on the Serbs. You explained why. Now, tell us, was the HVO capable, in the Lasva River Valley, of carrying out offensive operations towards the BH Army to cleanse the Central Bosnia area of the Muslims and have an ethnically-pure territory?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I said "incapable," I spoke of the enemy that I had to contend with on a daily basis. I had no thoughts about any attacks on the Muslims. I don't know what you're actually asking me. I could not have any idea of this. People were living there in that area. People were doing the best they could to survive. So no attacks. All the manoeuvres going on -- only forces engaged in manoeuvres could attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me a follow-up question, because you are the first witness who was clear enough, as far as I can see, on something that could be quite essential. I was listening to you carefully. You told us that there was a front-line. We keep this in mind. And behind the front-line, there were the Serbs. On the front-line, there was the HVO and there was the ABiH. And you said that there was a defence line that was about one or two kilometres' long. So you can see the front-line -- what a pity we didn't think of having a map, because I could have asked you to draw it all and to mark it all on the map. There was a defence line that was about one to two kilometres' long, and then there's the in-depth territory. And you say that in depth there were the soldiers that would go home, that would go work in the fields or have a rest, and then return to the front-line. Ms. Alaburic put to you a question about the in-depth territory or the notion of "in-depth." In that so-called "in-depth" area, there were the ABiH and the HVO; is that so? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The defence line was two kilometres' long -- or two kilometres in depth and hundred kilometres long, so it was only two kilometres in depth from the front. Everything else was the depth of the population, the units, and so on. So I'm talking about in-depth as compared to the front-line. So it is within that depth that all the units, the BH Army and HVO units, were located. Most of them -- 90 per cent of these soldiers were in their houses, in their own homes, except for those who were refugees and had no homes to go to, and where in the Krajina Brigade, the El Mujahid, the 7th Muslim, they were in the barracks, whether they -- the barracks in Zenica or Travnik. Everybody else was at home in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've added something else. You're telling us that there was the front-line, there was the defence line where the depth is, say, two kilometres, and then in -- and this is the specification you just added, in that defence line there was the HVO and the BiH Army, and then there's the whole lot, the remainder; the houses, the soldiers going back home, the rear, civilians -- well, you didn't say "civilians," but it could be concluded that the civilians were there, too, in the rear. And you added that there are also units, such as the Krajina Brigade, the Mujahid, or the 7th Muslim Brigades, that have their barracks. Is that a right summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because these are important concepts. Sometimes it's hard to really fathom what it is, and I think you are among the first witnesses who are clear enough on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this seems to be a good time for the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's move on to Novi Travnik, 1992, October 1992; Travnik, October 1992. For those acquainted with the indictment, we're dealing with paragraph 28. Tell us, please, General, in Novi Travnik was there an important factory there at all?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an important factory for Yugoslavia and for Bosnia-Herzegovina, manufacturing high-calibre artillery and tank weapons. It was called Bratstvo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had access to the factory?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Both Croats and Muslims had access there, because there were no Serb villages in the surrounding parts. And the JNA, in February 1992, attempted to take out finished goods from the Bratstvo factory. However, thanks to the members of the Croatian population, they prevented them from taking weapons away, which could have been taken to Croatia at the time. So the weapons remained in the Bratstvo factory. When I arrived, I realised the importance that the factory had, and I did my best to disperse the weapons away from the factory. And I learned from the managing directors how much equipment there was there, how many weapons, and then I discussed this with the decision-makers both on the Muslim and Croat side about the dispersion of these weapons, because neither side could pull them out without everybody knowing about it. So I decide -- we made a decision to send a third to the southern front, where the Croats and Muslims acted together, and then for the TO, for the BH Army, a third was to go to them for the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then another third to me for my area of responsibility, and that last third would be divided 50:50. So realising the importance of the Bratstvo factory, I solved the problem and equipped people with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, when you say a third stayed for the local requirements and then was divided 50:50, half/half, half/half to whom, between which sides?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO and the Territorial Defence at the time, as organisational forms in which the population was involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, was there anything that happened in June 1992 with respect to this factory?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In June, we referred to this as the first conflict where there were dead and wounded between the Croats and Muslims, or HVO and BH Army, for supremacy. It was a fight for supremacy over the factory. And, in fact, the Muslims managed to eliminate the HVO -- or, rather, the Croats, eliminate them from the factory, and the Croats no longer had access to the factory. There was just one position from which you could see the factory, but you couldn't approach the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was this position called from which you could see the factory?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We referred to it as the relay, because there was, in fact, a small tower for the local television station, and it was a prominent position visible from the surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at a few documents on the situation in Novi Travnik in October 1992. The first document is 4D895, which is a consolidated report for the 19th of October, and let's look at item 3, the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, a report from Novi Travnik. And it says, and I quote: "In the evening hours on the 18th of October, 1992, there was a serious deterioration in relations between the Muslims and Croats, the HVO and BH Army, and this escalated to an all-out conflict in which a member of the BH Army was killed and a member of the HVO was wounded by sniper fire." Now, my question to you, General, is this: This description of events in Novi Travnik for that day, is that correct, was that what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was correct. But I'd just like to say that this incident or, rather, the conflict took place on this repeater station because some parts of the BH Army -- some members of the BH Army attempted to gain control of that position, which was a strong topographical position, in order to make it impossible for the HVO even to see the factory. There were three or four soldiers at that particular vantage point, and they managed to hold the position for a time, and this relates to the person who was wounded and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D896. It's page 4 of the Croatian, General, and point 2 relating to the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. It's a report from Vitez, at 1545 hours, for the 20th of October, 1992. And among other things, General, here it says that: "The opposite side, the Territorial Defence, is proposing that we issue an order urgently for a cease-fire and to undertake negotiations, and it is our position a cease-fire with unconditional surrender of Commander of the Territorial Defence, Refik Lendo." And now Tihomir Blaskic is asking for permission to act in that manner, and then it goes on to say that: "Ivica Stojak [realtime transcript read in error "Stojic"], who was seriously wounded, member of the Municipal Staff of Travnik, succumbed to his wounds." Now, let's see about this truce and Refik Lendo. Now, General, did you know about this, that it was one of the conditions laid down by the HVO for a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So far, I've said about the situation at the repeater location, in the evening hours of the 18th, then on the 19th there are intense combat activities. I strengthened the defence lines there, new units I introduced. I personally was there throughout that day's fighting, but now that conflict spreads along the lines or in depth of the territory. At many points, conflicts flare up. The situation is becoming critical, in my opinion. Both sides, and I'm referring to higher echelons, so primarily in the BiH Army, they realised that they have not achieved their goal, and that now they insist on negotiations. We say, Yes, negotiations, but we want for you to surrender Refik Lendo, who is responsible for tens of casualties. And I made a decision for a funeral to take part in night-time, and for months in the Lasva Valley such funerals would take part during night-time because this whole territory could be seen by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct the name, fourth line on the 77 page. The name entered is incorrect. The correct name is "Ivica Stojak," not "Ivica Stojic." So, General, Ivica Stojak, was that the predecessor of the commander of the Travnik Brigade, would that be your predecessor in the Travnik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as I said, the conflict spreads into the depth of the territory. Ivica Stojak was killed at the check-point Karnada [phoen], which is when you leave Novi Travnik. He was the first commander in Travnik and throughout that time had been commander of the Municipal Crisis Staff and later on commander of the brigade. And because of his death, as I explained earlier, I had to take over the command post of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We did not refer to him by name at that previous time, and now I'm going to try and be more precise. Later on in this report, with reference to the situation in Novi Travnik, it's stated: "Muslim forces do not allow our ambulance vehicles to transfer the casualties to the hospital, and most of those who died died en route to the hospital, and in certain cases members of the TO units even put hand-grenades into the mouths of some of them and taunted them at the barricades." Is that part correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Travnik hospital served all those in that area, and it was the only hospital from Jajce to Busovaca and Vitez. And when the conflict around the repeater station spread, one of the ramifications of that was the killing of Stojak, it was a major ramification, but another was that our wounded had no place to be treated at. And this is the time when we ordered that a hospital be opened up at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you another question, General, the first part of your answer did not enter the transcript. Is that part that I quoted from, was that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that part of that report was correct? That was my question. Please, General, briefly tell us, that part referring to hand-grenades in mouths, did you hear at the time that a patient was put a hand-grenade into mouth?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was correct or not, but I had a barrel of a gun put into my mouth. This is what I referred to as incidents. But this was a new dimension. Up to that point, ambulance vehicles could pass through check-points on both sides, but this was the first time when an ambulance could not pass a certain check-point bearing a patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next document, 4D897. It is referred to as Central Bosnia Operational Zone, 21st of October, report at 2100 hours, and it's stated for the Novi Travnik battle zone, Muslim forces continue heavy artillery shelling on the town, itself, using mostly Howitzers, 122 millimetres. Would that statement be true, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Bratstvo did produce and manufacture such equipment. As I stated earlier, they received half of one-third, and we could precisely state what kind of artillery was used. So this part is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It is also stated in the report that the enemy had disarmed HVO units in villages where the number of currents [as interpreted] was negligible, such as the villages of Kopila, Torine, et cetera, et cetera. Let me not list all of these. To the best of your knowledge, was this statement about disarming them correct or not?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I, personally, in front of the old hotel in Novi Travnik, I encountered refugees from the village of Senkovici. It is a mixed-population village, and it is located en route between Novi Travnik and Bugojno. In that action, three, four villages were cleansed. Most people came from Senkovici because that village was most important for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Later on in this report, under item 5, referring to HVO units, it is stated: "In Vitez, there is a barracks in the village of Ahmici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you have just stated that Senkovici was important for your purposes. Could you specify what your purposes were and why this village was important for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was important because I had to have communication with the HVO in Bugojno. I could not have a situation where just one side had communication, in this case TO or the BiH Army, particularly in circumstances when the 7th Muslim Brigade and Mujahedin held the Rostovo point, which means that my communication with Bugojno had been disconnected, effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Filipovic, whether Senkovici was in majority inhabited by Croats or by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a mixed-population village, a majority Muslim, but quite a large portion were Croats. And in terms of hamlets around that village, some hamlets were occupied by Muslims, some inhabited by Croats, but it was a majority Muslim village, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was the ethnic composition a factor that you took into account when you examined the situation in a tactical perspective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the start of the war, I had maps, and wherever I would come, I would indicate on the map the ethnic composition; red for Serbs, green for Muslims, and blue for Croats. It was important who lived where in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was important for me because this was the only route to Bugojno that was which was not now disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for interrupting, but for a couple of minutes we don't have the transcript on our monitors; not only me, but everybody around. We do have LiveNote, but we are marking the transcript and we need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technicians are about to come, but we can continue, can't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I think the witness was still in the process of answering my question, and I don't see why he should not be allowed to continue. Witness, you had said at the beginning you had a map where you put colours for the composition -- the ethnic composition of places, red for Serbs, et cetera. It was important to you, you said, because this was the only route to Bugojno that was not now disrupted. My question had been whether you did take into account, in your tactical planning of operations, this ethnical composition, and you have given a first answer. But would you please go on and answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated at the beginning of the war I had to know, because I commanded a large area. Senkovici were probably underlined by the blue and the green colours. But in technical terms, my communication with Bugojno had been very difficult, and had the Croats left Senkovici, then I no longer can even think about gaining access through that area. I would have liked for the whole area to be populated by Croats, but it simply wasn't so. I don't know tactically what you mean. When that happened, I knew that further communication was impossible from that point on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, by "tactical" I mean when you are faced with a situation where, as a commander, you have to take a decision, you make an analysis. You analyse the enemy situation, your own tasks, the terrain, the weather, and so forth. This is a ritual which you are better familiar with than myself. And when you look at the terrain, would the ethnic composition of a town be an element that you would also take into account? And if so, would it be important or would it be only in extreme cases that it would prompt you to take one decision rather than another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole time, it was important to me. And at times when it's a make-or-break situation, then it becomes decisive. Had I attacked, then I would have tried to discard all possibilities of having them place a check-point in Senkovici to prevent me from passing. And that's what the Muslim side did, too. So since there was a conflict on, the conflict was expanding, they eliminated the danger in Senkovici, Torine, and wherever else, but Senkovici were more important because they were along the communication line along the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I didn't mean to interrupt the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's go back to our report, which is document 4D897. And we're now referring to the portion where the village of Ahmici is mentioned, and it says that in Vitez, the barricades in Ahmici village on the main motorway from Busovaca to Vitez have been completely smashed, and the Muslim forces had been driven out of the village and completely routed. The Muslim forces, at their own initiative, handed over their weapons. Now, my question to you, General, is this: It says here that the village of Ahmici was on the main road from Busovaca to Vitez. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I know the terrain in detail, Ahmici is one and a half kilometres away from the road. The mosque is up there, and the cemetery, but 25 years prior to the war, with the fact that the area became more built up, the village did descend down to the highway. But as far as I know, it was Santici, a Croatian village, where as Ahmici was a Muslim village. So the new houses that were built provided the possibility of going out onto the main road, and the main road was 10 to 15 minutes -- 10 to 15 metres from the houses. And Santici was the most sensitive point between Busovaca and Vitez, as far as the Croats were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you repeat the last sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Ahmici were [as interpreted] a position -- or, rather, Santici was a position which was the most sensitive of the interruption of communication between Busovaca and Vitez, and all the daily comings and goings, so that was the most sensitive point as far as that road and that communication line was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, the village of Ahmici was left out of the transcript. That's why I asked you to repeat the sentence. Tell me now, at that position, Ahmici-Santici, what was the breadth of territory, the width of the territory, which in 1992 and in 1993 was under the control of the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, we found that width to be 800 metres, but topographically speaking, that's it, the Lasva Valley. But when there was no conflict, then the breadth is even greater. But let me repeat, where you had exclusively Croats, that is a breadth of 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, if you were Mehmed Alagic at the time, if you were in his position and had the task of cutting across the Busovaca-Vitez communication line, what point would it be that you would choose to do that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I were in Mehmed Alagic's position, the only place where you could do that successfully, without any large units, would be Ahmici and Santici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, carrying on from that, General, let's look at item 8, where it says that the HVO suffered the following losses: 10 killed, 32 wounded, and 5 confirmed missing. And then it goes on to say that they no longer needed reinforcement in manpower, which they had asked for -- which the Main Staff had asked for previously, the HVO Main Staff, that is. And then it says that the forces that you sent and that arrived and reached Prozor might be held there for a time or sent back. Now, to the best of your knowledge, General, at that time, and we're dealing with the 21st of October, was the situation calming down so that no reinforcement was necessary from outside? Is that portion of the report correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After two days of intensive fighting, along with the losses mentioned here, but I'm not sure that all the losses are incorporated there, anyway, all the defence across Jajce to Travnik and Zenica was being broken, especially Jajce was the key point. Then both the Muslim side and our side was doing everything in its power to deal with the conflict as best they could. So the information here is correct, given the time and period. Well, we asked for reinforcements at the beginning of the conflict, when it wasn't just an incident but when we saw that it was an all-out conflict, so we asked for reinforcements. But when the Muslim side didn't manage to affect its target, especially when it came to the relay station, but, yes, it did with respect to the Bugojno-Novi Travnik area, then we no longer needed assistance, we no longer needed reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, General. It is P644, and it is an order for a cease-fire, dated the 24th of October, 1992, issued by the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, sent to Travnik, among others. Tell us, General, did this order for a cease-fire reach you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the order did reach me. Now, since I was in the military district, it would have been in this form. If I was in Travnik, it would have come in from Blaskic for the brigade in Travnik. But, anyway, it did reach me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on your territory, was there a cease-fire even before this order?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After an all-out conflict -- well, an incident and conflict and so many dead, we needed days after that to deal with the situation, which was particularly sensitive in Travnik because of Stojak's death.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at what you've just said by looking at the next document, 4D1179, which is a consolidated report for the 25th from the operative zone. They are reporting that they have received the order on a cease-fire, which we were looking at a moment ago, and this can be seen from the reference numbers and so on, and it says that the Muslim forces, despite the order from the chief of the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence, on the 24th of October opened fire with mortars targeting the town, and at the Streliste facility or firing range, they kept firing for 20 rounds in 30 minutes and snipers were also active. So is that part of the report correct about the sporadic shooting in Novi Travnik and what happened on that particular day, the 24th of October?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I was in Novi Travnik at that time. Otherwise, I would know all about this in detail. This does not incorporate what my men fired, because as I said, with the calming down of the situation, this went on for a number of days. Orders could be issued, but you needed time for the situation to actually calm down, what with people having been killed and people losing their nearest and dearest, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now let's move on to Busovaca. January 1993 is the date. And for that, let's look at the first document which deals with this; 4D392 is the number. Yes, 4D392. This is an assessment -- a security assessment of the situation from the Armed Forces of BH. It says the security organ of the 3rd Corps is of the opinion that the forces of the BH Army in this area, if there were to be a serious clash, could successfully fight back the HVO's forces, on the condition that the BH Army cuts off the road communications or the communication line from Busovaca, Kiseljak, Fojnica, at Lugovi and Kacuni -- that the BH Army should cut off the communication lines running from Busovaca-Kiseljak to Fojnica at Lugovi and Kacuni, and also the road from Busovaca to Vitez, Busovaca-Vitez, and Vitez-Travnik at Mecave, and that ammunition and grenades should be sent to the area as soon as possible. Now, may we have a map on e-court. 4D2014 is the number. And I'm going to ask you, General, to indicate for us on that map where the communication along the Lasva River Valley lines were supposed to be cut. May we have the usher's assistance in providing the witness with a felt pen so that he can draw on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a little technical problem with this map also. I'm going to have to print out a hard copy of the map so the witness can mark on it. Is that okay, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we need to do that, then I can hand the witness my copy, although those places are already marked, to avoid interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We would also like to have it. It is not in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, it's not in the binder because this will be an IC map, and I thought that we'd be able to do it all through e-court because the witness has not prepared any markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, would it be possible to put this issue aside for tomorrow morning and to have maps provided to whoever in the courtroom would like to have them? I'm sure the Judges would for tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. A constructive proposal, as always. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let's leave those maps for the moment.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: May I say something? Can I just tell you which those places are?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that in due course when we have the map, because we didn't mention the places where the Busovaca-Vitez road was cut. So let's move on to the next document, which is P1200. This is an assessment of the situation compiled by the commander of the 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic. Please, General, under item 4, take a look, and it states here -- the heading "The Roads of Evacuation and Delivery." It reads: "According to our personal assessments, all roads can be put under the control of BiH Army, except for the road Vitez-Travnik, because along the whole direction it borders the places impossible to control for the BH Army." General, could you please explain to us this assessment by Mr. Hadzihasanovic? Why is it impossible for the BiH Army to control this section of the road?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In respect to the previous document, that it was generated from the Supreme Command of the BiH Army, and this one -- the present document comes from the 3rd Corps, so they say they can control everything except for this between Vitez and Travnik, but they could -- if you take Travnik in a broader sense, they could do so at the eastern-most boundary of Travnik. But in terms of communication between Vitez and Travnik, until the very entrance to Travnik, it was impossible for them to do so because of the composition of the inhabitants, even in terms of military activities had they been in a position to effect defence operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this ethnic composition which precludes the army to control that communication?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from that point to Ahmici, inclusively, and Vitez, there is not a single Muslim village or any groups of newly-built homes along the road where -- inhabited by Muslims where they could organise a cessation of firing of either high or low intensity. In Bosnia, for instance, if you had a hamlet within a village inhabited by a certain group, that would give the right for the whole group to fight for the whole village. If there are none of your members in a village, then there would be no justification. For instance, in the war between Serbia and Slovenia, since there were no Serbs in Slovenia, Serbs allowed Slovenia to secede from Yugoslavia. This is how I saw the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's put Slovenia aside for a while. Let's go back to the assessment of Enver Hadzihasanovic. You say that this meant that there was Croatian villages along that road, and for that reason the BiH Army could not control that road; is this what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I meant to say. I apologise for the digressions that I make. I simply lose sense of time sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please, to the best of your knowledge, did Enver Hadzihasanovic and did other Muslim commanders take into account which village was Muslim, which village was Croatian, and which were mixed?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Without a doubt. The same conclusion could have been done by somebody in Sarajevo or the -- Loncarevic in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Referring to Judge Trechsel's question of you being mindful of the ethnic composition of villages, could you tell us, was that composition objectively important in terms of controlling certain area, territory, or communications, and reliance on the local population, did it mean something in the doctrine of defence that was applied?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said it was an important factor. The personnel, the men, are barracked at their own homes deep in the territory, and they can be put into action. For a goal -- an offensive goal to be able to be effective, you had to have a manoeuvring unit, and the composition of the people under arms was, of course, very important in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next document, 421207 -- 4D1207. This is a report from the defence staff of Zenica municipality. It comes from the Muslim side, and it's stated here that there was fighting in the village of Dusina between members of the army and the HVO in the morning hours on 26th of January, 1993. And in this fighting, three HVO members were killed, another three were wounded, and five or six were captured. Is this statement about the fighting at the Dusina village on that date correct or truthful or not?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that they liquidated the HVO and the Croats from the village of Dusina. I'm not sure whether there was any fighting, and those captured were later dead or killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say later on those captured were dead, could you please explain the cause of their death, despite the words that appears in the English translation? What was the cause of their death?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They were executed later on, they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, who killed those HVO members?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, in Busovaca, I don't know the serial number of the brigade, there were parts of the 7th Muslim Brigade in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's take a look at the next document, 4D1210. This document, and this is a public announcement by the 3rd Corps Press Centre, the situation is portrayed differently. In the military report, we have that HVO forces were busted, and in this public announcement it is stated that HVO forces are encircled. Now, I correct myself. The inhabitants of the villages of Dusina, Gornja Visnjica and Brdo are now surrounded by HVO forces. General, when you compare, and if you could remember, the previous military report and this public announcement, what would you say? Would this public announcement be truthful, in terms of how things are portrayed to the public, or is this distorted?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a propaganda warfare, where the situation is depicted opposite to the reality. Three villages -- I repeat, three villages were cleansed in that area. Ten members of the HVO were killed; not in fighting, but they were executed. And for their public, they are stating that villages are encircled by HVO, which means that Croats killed themselves. The bottom line, it's propaganda warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the next paragraph. It mentions conflicts within the HVO forces, and Zvonko Rajic and another six extremists are referred to. To the best of your knowledge, was their demise the result of conflicts between their ranks or were they executed by the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were executed, and they have to justify somehow not just the executions, but the fact that they expelled three Croats from three villages and now they are inventing this conflict among HVO forces. Who the three brothers -- I had a sister of those three brothers coming to me, trying to get me to intervene and bring the responsible persons to book, but this notion is quite interesting. Internal conflicts within the HVO, so they can whitewash and hide the fact that there were people killed, but now they are explaining that away by internal conflicts within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to skip the next document, because it requires us to make markings on a map, so we will deal with it tomorrow. Let's take a look at document 4D1206.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, maybe it would be best to continue tomorrow. Let me tell you that you have used up two hours and ten minutes so far. You have one hour and fifty minutes left. There are a great number of documents. Please be selective in your use of documents. Witness, let me remind you of the basic instructions I already told you about. You are not to talk to anyone about the substance of this hearing. We're sitting tomorrow in the afternoon, which means that we are expecting you for 2.15. I hope we'll be able to start on time at 2.15 sharp and that we will not have to wait, which is a very unfortunate habit we've been running into lately. I wish you all a pleasant evening, and see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
